name: style-plain
title: Plain English
description:
Plain English, as something a document can be measured against. Choose this profile if you want everyday words, a named actor in front of the verb, one idea to a sentence, and the reader addressed as "you". A finding means the document sits outside that register, which is a statement about fit and not a defect.

Ten rules, drawn from three published guides: the Federal Plain Language Guidelines (March 2011, Revision 1 May 2011), written by the Plain Language Action and Information Network and now hosted at digital.gov after plainlanguage.gov was folded into it; the GOV.UK style guide, now at guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk; and the Plain English Campaign's "How to write in plain English". Where a guide gives a number, that number was the starting point; where it survived measurement against writing in this register it is the edge and the rule says so, and where it did not the rule says that instead and gives the measured edge. One published figure did not survive: see style-plain-sentence-length-short. Eleven of the guides' recommendations turned out to be expressible as a rate or as sentence-length variation; several more did not, and are listed under notMechanised below rather than shipped as weak rules. Two corpora sit behind the numbers, and every rule reports against both: 21 documents of published plain-language writing, which is in register and says whether an edge reports the register itself, and 18 documents of engineering documentation, which is out of register and says how wide the gap is. Every edge here is still somebody else's number: retune them against prose in the register you actually want.

corpus.note: Two corpora. The in-register corpus is 21 documents / 26,224 words of published plain-language writing: 14 chapters of the Mailchimp Content Style Guide, three Mailchimp help-centre articles, Basecamp's "Getting Real", two "Shape Up" chapters and Basecamp's internal communication guide. Twenty of the 21 (25,121 words) clear the prose gate; "Getting Real" does not, at 78.8 words per apparent sentence, because it is extracted as a page of chapter links. That corpus answers the question an off-register corpus cannot: whether an edge reports the register it is supposed to describe. Two edges moved because of it and one moved because of a related measurement, and the rules say which. The local corpus is 16 documents / 19,555 words of human-written engineering documentation under /home/bas/Downloads: every file of 250 words or more that clears the engine's default prose gate. It is out of register by construction and is here to show the size of the gap, not the centre of the band. An earlier draft of this profile widened the gate to maxSentenceWords 200 and minSentenceWords 1 and measured 18 local documents instead of 16. The two extra ones were a Python source file pasted into a .txt and a README that is headings, bullets and code fences, at 79.5 and 135.8 words per apparent sentence; between them they produced 4 of the profile's 24 findings, including a report that a Python module addresses its reader too rarely. The gate is back at the engine default. Two kinds of noise survive it. Markdown and HTML tables are extracted as running text, so their cells count as words with no full stop at the end and pull the apparent sentence length up; --skip-tables is the right setting for documentation. And a file that mixes prose with console output or version strings is measured as one document, because a file extension followed by a space reads as the end of a sentence. Quantiles are linear-interpolated; min and max are the observed extremes. These numbers are the first thing to retune.

voice: Short sentences of varied length, averaging somewhere between 10 and 25 words. Active verbs with a named actor. The reader is "you" and the writer is "we". Everyday words where the formal one has an everyday equal. One idea to a sentence.
notMechanised: Paragraph length ("no more than 150 words in three to eight sentences"): extraction hands the engine a flat text stream and no detector kind counts paragraphs, so this is not expressible.

The limit of two or three abbreviations per document: the limit is on distinct abbreviations, and density counts occurrences, not types. A rate of all-caps tokens was measured and reached 58.8 per 1000 words in the local corpus, leaving no room between ordinary technical prose and any defensible edge.
Defining an abbreviation on first use: this is a relation between two positions in a document and no kind expresses it.

Contractions: the sources point in opposite directions. The Federal guidelines ask for them ("Use contractions when appropriate"); GOV.UK asks against the negative ones ("Use cannot, instead of can't"). A band would have to pick a side the guidance does not.

One idea to a sentence, keeping subject and verb close, double negatives, doublets such as "cease and desist", noun strings, and slashes: these are spans, and a style profile is bands only, because a span rule can hide another set's finding underneath it. They belong in an ordinary rule set selected on its own.
Headings, lists, tables and examples: layout, not rate.

A ceiling on sentence-length variation - a rhythm rule with params.minCV, which style-academic, style-newsroom and style-economist all ship, and the obvious way to make style-plain-rhythm-even two-sided. Two reasons it is not here. The guides ask for variation and nowhere object to too much of it, so there is no number to take. And the measurement argues against inventing one: in both corpora the documents with the highest variation are the ones whose extracted text carries headings and list items, which the sentence splitter counts as very short sentences. The local maximum of 1.54 is an HTML page of shell transcripts and code blocks and the in-register maximum of 1.76 is a help-centre page of tables, while the prose that actually lurches sits in the middle of the distribution. A ceiling there would report layout, not rhythm. The long half of the two-sided constraint is carried by style-plain-sentence-length-long instead, which reads the mean rather than the spread and is not fooled the same way.

tension.note: economist/paren-scarcity reports a document that uses no parentheses at all (params.max 0). Prose written to this register often has none: short sentences carrying one idea each rarely need an aside. Measured, and this is the sharpest tension in the set: of every rule in every non-style set in this repository, paren-scarcity is the only one that reports on this profile's own on-target fixture, the document that defines what being in this register looks like. Both readings stand and neither is evidence about the other. If you disagree with that one for your own writing, put it in the ignore list of your own slop.json.

economist/comma-scarcity reports a document under 20 commas per 1000 words. Cutting subordination to reach an average of 10 to 25 words a sentence lowers the comma rate, so the two pull against each other at the short end of this band. Measured: this profile's choppy fixture runs 3 commas per 1000 words and reports there; its on-target fixture runs 44 and does not. The pull is real but it bites outside this profile's band rather than inside it.

humanizer-de/uniform-sentence-length reads sentence-length variation at cv 0.40 and, since this review, so does style-plain-rhythm-even. The two edges were derived separately, from different corpora, for different purposes, and they landed on the same number; a document that reports under one reports under the other. That is agreement, not duplication, but if you run both sets you will see the same document twice.

economist/long-sentences is the same metric as style-plain-sentence-length-long, with the same pattern and the same direction, at params.max 20 against this profile's 40. They compose: 20 to 40 endings per 1000 words is this profile's reading alone, and below 20 both apply and agree. Two differences worth knowing: the economist rule gates at maxSentenceWords 120 where this one gates at the engine default 60, and this one counts endings with a tightened pattern, so on a document full of numbered headings the two will disagree slightly about the rate.

economist/nominalisation-pileup reads the same metric at params.min 70 against this profile's 65, with a slightly wider ending list. They compose: 65 to 70 is this profile's reading alone and above 70 both apply. The edge was placed under 70 on purpose so that the two stack rather than collide.

wikipedia-ai/note-that is a shipped, default-on rule, and one arm of its pattern is "it should be noted", which is also one of the 25 phrases in style-plain-wordy-phrase-high. Same direction, different shape: the shipped rule marks each occurrence as a span, this profile only reports when the whole document carries at least two circumlocutions at 4 per 1000 words. A document heavy in that phrase gets both readings, which is correct. Nothing is masked either way, because every rule in this profile is document-level and has no span to collapse another set's finding into.

slop-gate/leverage matches "leverage", which is also in the style-plain-formal-word-high list, taken from the GOV.UK words-to-replace table. Same direction, different shape: a span there, a component of a document rate here. Running both sets double-counts the word.

slop-gate/empower matches "empower", which is also in the style-plain-formal-word-high list, from the same GOV.UK table. Measured: this profile's bureaucratic fixture reports under both. Same direction, so the two compose rather than conflict, but the word is counted twice.

slop-gate/streamline matches "streamline", the third word this profile's formal-word list shares with slop-gate. Same direction and the same double-count. If you run slop-gate and this profile together and want each word read once, ignore the three slop-gate rules rather than editing this list, because the list is quoted from a published source and the rate depends on all of it.

rules.name: Sentence length outside the range this register keeps
rules.description: Sentence endings per 1000 words, which is average sentence length turned upside down. Below the band the average sentence runs 25 words or longer, which GOV.UK names as the point to look at a sentence again; above it the page reads as separate statements rather than connected prose.
rules.suggest: Outside the plain band (40 to 100 sentence endings per 1000 words, an average of 10 to 25 words a sentence). Below it, split the longest sentences so each carries one idea. Above it, join the shortest statements into sentences that each carry one idea.
rules.note: A measurement of fit: reference material and analysis sit below the band and read perfectly well, and release notes and staccato incident write-ups sit above it on purpose. GOV.UK: "Do not use long sentences. Check sentences with more than 25 words to see if you can split them to make them clearer." The Federal Plain Language Guidelines have a section on short sentences but give no number. Three things about the measurement, all of them departures from the other style profiles. The pattern is not the bare [.!?](?=\s|$) they share: it also requires a non-space character before the stop and declines a stop that closes a number at the start of a line, because inline code stripped out of HTML leaves a full stop standing on its own and a numbered heading leaves one after the number. The pattern is shared with style-plain-sentence-length-short, and it is at the short edge that the difference showed: those two artefacts supplied 26% and 33% of the counted endings in the only two local documents that reported there, so both reports were markup rather than prose. Away from those two the change is small: it moves the counted rate by at most 7.8% on any other local document, and by nothing at all on six of them. Because this rule and the prose gate read the same quantity, the gate is also this rule's own ceiling: above an average of 60 words between full stops the engine stops treating the text as prose, so this rule reports averages between 25 and 60 words a sentence and says nothing above that. And params.minSentences is 15 rather than the default 5, because an average over five sentences is not an average: the four local documents with the fewest sentences were also the four with the longest apparent sentences, and all four are bulleted lists whose items carry words but no full stops. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: band 40-100 /1000; this edge is params.max 40. Published number, not a percentile: GOV.UK's 25-word figure. In-register corpus, 20 measurable documents: 25.1 (min) / 51.1 (p25) / 58 (median) / 81.6 (p90) / 120 (max); 1 of the 20 sits at or below the edge, a help-centre page whose text is mostly a table. Local corpus, 16 documents: 17.3 (min) / 30.1 (p25) / 45.5 (median) / 55.3 (p90) / 63.1 (max); 3 of 16 report. An earlier draft ran with the widened gate and minSentences 5 and reported 8 of 18 local documents; five of those eight were a Python file, a bulleted README, a table-shaped README and two copies of a bullet-and-table issue write-up.  Upper edge: band 40-100 /1000; this edge is params.min 100. Corpus-derived, and it replaces a published number that measurement rejected. In-register corpus, 20 measurable documents: 25.1 (min) / 58 (median) / 70.3 (p75) / 81.6 (p90) / 120 (max). The edge sits above p90 and above every in-register document but one, a 275-word page of bulleted principles whose items average 8.3 words. At the published 67 the rule reported 6 of those 20. Local corpus, 16 documents: max 63.1, so nothing reports; at 67 it reported 2 of 18, and both of those were markup artefacts rather than short sentences.  The sentence gate is 8, from the long edge. The short edge carried 15 before the two were merged, but that gate could never bind: firing at 100 endings per 1000 over the 250-word minimum already means 25 sentences. Applied to the long edge, 15 would have blocked every document between 250 and 375 words, because prose long-winded enough to reach that edge has few sentences by construction.

hit: The team decided at the end of the review that the migration would run in three stages rather than as a single cutover, mostly because the earlier attempt had shown how quickly a partial failure could leave the two databases disagreeing about the same account. In the first stage, which ran for six weeks over the summer, every write was mirrored to the new cluster while reads carried on being served from the old one, and a background job compared the two copies row by row. That job wrote a report each morning, which the engineer on call read before the daily meeting started, and the report was noisy at first, largely because of timestamp rounding in a column nobody had looked at since the schema was written. It took the better part of a fortnight to work out which of the differences were real and which were an artefact of the comparison itself, and only then did the numbers start to mean anything. Once the report settled to a handful of rows a day, all of them explained by a known race in the ingest path, the team moved on to the second stage and shifted a small share of read traffic to the new cluster. Latency and error rates were watched on a dashboard that had been built for the migration and was thrown away afterwards, which is the fate of most tooling written under that kind of deadline. The third stage was the cutover itself, and it was deliberately dull, with the share raised from ten per cent to fifty over a week and then to a hundred over a quiet weekend in October. The old cluster was left running in a read-only mode for a further month, in case something turned up that nobody on the team had thought of during the planning that preceded the work. Nothing did turn up, which the team took as evidence that the slow approach had been worth the two extra months that it cost the roadmap, although not everybody agreed with that reading of the outcome. One engineer argued afterwards that the same result could have been reached in half the time with a better comparison tool and rather less caution about a race that had already been understood. The argument was never settled. The next migration was planned in much the same way, because the people who had lived through the first one were also the people who ended up writing the second plan. The plan that came out of that review ran to eleven pages, and most of that length was a list of the things that could go wrong at each stage together with the name of the person who would notice them first. Two of those eleven pages covered the rollback, which nobody expected to use and which the team rehearsed twice anyway, once on a Tuesday afternoon with the whole group watching and once at four in the morning with a single engineer on a laptop. The overnight run was the one that found the problem, because the script that flipped the read traffic back assumed a hostname that only existed while the mirroring job was still running on the old cluster. That assumption came into the script from somebody who had since left the team, and it had been right on the day somebody typed it, which is how most of these things start. The fix took an hour and the argument about whether to write it down took the rest of the morning, since the group could not agree on where a note like that belongs once a migration is over and the cluster it describes has gone. In the end the note went into the runbook for the new cluster, where anybody looking for it would have no reason to be, and also into the commit message, where it has stayed readable ever since. The second stage overlapped with a quarter close, which meant the finance team was reading from the same tables at the same moment as the comparison job, and the two workloads did not sit together comfortably. Nobody had thought to ask about the quarter close during planning, and the lesson the team took from that week was less about databases than about who gets invited to the meeting where somebody picks the dates.

The build failed and nobody knew why. The log came back empty. We checked the runner and it looked healthy. We checked the cache and it was cold. That seemed odd to us. A cold cache is slow, not fatal. So we looked at the step again. It had timed out after sixty seconds. The install takes ninety seconds. It has always taken ninety. The timeout was the new thing. Someone had lowered it last Thursday. They lowered it to catch a hang. The hang was real enough. The fix pointed at the wrong thing. We raised the timeout and the build passed. Then we went looking for the hang. It sat in a post-install script. The script waited on a lock. The cache held that lock. A cold cache made the lock slow. The two bugs turned out to be one bug. We fixed the script for good. We left the timeout where it was. The build has passed every day since. Nobody has touched that config. Quiet is usually a good sign. It is not always a good sign. So we added a metric for it. The metric tracks install time. It alerts above two minutes. Nothing has alerted so far. The graph has stayed flat. Flat graphs are boring to look at. Boring was the point of the work. The runbook is much shorter now. It says one thing only. Check the install step first. That advice is dull to read. It is also correct. Most advice is one or the other. We wrote it down anyway. The next person will thank us. Or they will not thank us. Either way the note is there. It cost ten minutes to write. The bug had cost two days. That trade is an easy one. We should make it more often. We rarely do make it. There is always another ticket waiting. The note gets written later. Later has a way of never coming. This time it came.
miss: You can claim a travel grant if you work for a public body and your trip supports a project we already fund. Read this page first. It tells you what to send, how long each step takes, and who to ask when something goes wrong along the way. Your trip qualifies if it lasts fewer than 14 days and your manager has signed the request form before you book anything at all. Ask your finance team if you are not sure. They answer most questions the same day, and they will tell you straight away if the trip falls outside the rules, which saves you the trouble of filling in a form that we would only have to send back. Next, gather your papers. You need the signed form, a quote for the travel, and a short note that says why the trip matters to the work you do. Scan all three and send them to the grants inbox as a single file. We reply within 10 working days. If we need more from you, we will say what is missing and give you a date to send it by, so you are never left guessing at the end of a long week, and we will never turn down a claim without telling you why. Once we approve the grant, we pay it into the account you gave us, and the money usually arrives within five working days. Keep your receipts. We may ask to see them for up to two years after you travel, and we cannot pay a second claim while an older one is still open on your record. If we turn your claim down, write to the same inbox within 28 days and tell us what you think we got wrong. A different officer will read the file and decide. You will hear back within 20 working days, and nothing in that review changes your rights under your contract with the department that employs you. We update this page every spring. Tell us if you find anything here that does not match what we do, because the page is only useful to you while it stays true.

rules.name: Sentences closer to one length than this register keeps them
rules.description: Sentence-length variation, as standard deviation over mean. Below the floor the sentences are close to a single length, which is what a page looks like when an average sentence length has been reached by making every sentence the same size.
rules.suggest: Below the plain floor (sentence-length variation 0.40). Let a three-word sentence land after a long one.
rules.note: A measurement of fit: prose in this state is correct and readable, and simply flatter than this register's rhythm. Plain English Campaign: "This does not mean making every sentence the same length. Be punchy. Vary your writing by mixing short sentences (like the last one) with longer ones (like this one)." The Federal Plain Language Guidelines make the same point about paragraphs. Neither attaches a number, so the edge is measured, and it is placed just under the flattest document in the in-register corpus at 0.41. That lands it on humanizer-de/uniform-sentence-length's 0.40, which was derived independently, from a different corpus, for a different purpose. The two now coincide: a document that reports here reports there too, and two derivations agreeing is worth more than a manufactured gap between them. An earlier draft used 0.45, placed under the minimum of the out-of-register corpus, and reported 2 of the 20 in-register documents. This rule has no ceiling on variation, which is a decision rather than an omission; notMechanised gives the measurement behind it. params.minSentences is 15 rather than the default 8, because a shape statistic over eight sentences is noise. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: floor cv 0.40. Corpus-derived: the guidance names varied sentence length and attaches no number to it. In-register corpus, 20 measurable documents: 0.41 (min) / 0.58 (p25) / 0.72 (median) / 1.63 (p90) / 1.76 (max); no document reports. Local corpus, 16 documents: 0.49 (min) / 0.78 (median) / 1.26 (p90) / 1.54 (max); no document reports. Not a dead rule: docs/web.md inside this repository runs cv 0.37 over 19 sentences and reports.

hit: The service reads a message from the queue and writes a row into the ledger table. The ledger keeps one row for every payment that the platform has ever handled. A second worker reads the ledger and builds a daily summary for each merchant. The summary job runs at two in the morning and finishes before the office opens. Support staff read the summary when a merchant calls about a missing payment. The summary shows the payment, the fee, and the date the money left us. Most calls are settled in under three minutes because the answer sits on one screen. The rest go to the payments team for a manual check against the ledger. That check means reading the raw message and comparing it with the bank statement. The statement arrives as a file at six in the morning on every working day. A separate job loads the file and matches each line against a ledger row. Lines that fail to match are written to an exceptions table for review. The exceptions table usually holds fewer than ten rows at the start of the day. A clerk works through them before lunch and closes each one with a note. Notes are kept for seven years because the regulator can ask to see them. The pipeline has run without a serious incident for the last nine months here. Small faults appear every few weeks and are cleared by the engineer on call. The team reviews the fault log at the end of every month in a meeting. Changes to the pipeline are made in the week after that meeting and never during it. The clerk keeps a short list of the merchants who appear in the table most often. That list goes to the account managers at the start of each quarter for a review.

rules.name: More passive constructions than this register uses
rules.description: A form of "to be" followed by a past participle, per 1000 words. Above the ceiling the document is built on constructions that leave the actor out, so a reader cannot see who does what.
rules.suggest: Above the plain ceiling (12 passive constructions per 1000 words). Name the actor and let it take the verb: "we will withhold your bond" for "bonds will be withheld".
rules.note: That two-part shape is the signature the Federal Plain Language Guidelines give for recognising a passive sentence. A measurement of fit, and the guidance itself keeps a place for the passive where the actor is the law or is genuinely unknown. The pattern is the shared one from the profile vocabulary. It reads participles by their -ed and -en endings, so it misses irregular ones ("is written", "was built") and picks up some adjectival forms ("is interested"). Both guides put active voice near the top of their lists: GOV.UK, "Use the active voice rather than the passive voice"; the Federal guidelines, "More than any other writing technique, using active voice and specifying who is performing an action will change the character of your writing." Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: ceiling 12 /1000. Corpus-derived. In-register corpus, 20 measurable documents: 0 (min) / 4.05 (median) / 6.82 (p90) / 9.8 (max); no document reports, and the edge sits 22% above the in-register maximum. Local corpus, 16 documents: 0 (min) / 2.3 (median) / 8.25 (p90) / 8.5 (max); no document reports. The Plain English Campaign's published target is a share of verbs ("aim to make about 80 to 90% of your verbs active"), which a rate per 1000 words only approximates; the two are not the same measurement and this edge does not come from that figure. There is no floor: no guide asks for a minimum of passive constructions, so there is no number to put there.

Approximately sixty per cent of the applications received in the preceding financial year were found to be deficient in one or more respects, which is quite unsatisfactory. Where an inconsistency is identified between the present procedure and the said instrument, the instrument shall prevail and the procedure will be amended accordingly by means of a further notification.
